messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ingrid is a 54-year-old married European-American woman who has worked as a head chef at a mid-sized restaurant for nearly two decades. She presented for intake following a referral from her primary care physician, reporting severe and persistent psychological distress following an assault committed by a male colleague she had known and trusted for several years. Her PCL-5 score of 68 places her in the severe range, and the picture that emerges across the first sessions is one of a woman whose interior world has been comprehensively reorganised around a single act of violence.

The assault occurred approximately fourteen months ago, after a late closing shift. The kitchen had emptied, and Ingrid was alone with the colleague finishing inventory — a routine she had repeated dozens of times without incident. What happened that night resists her own narration. She cannot sequence it, cannot find words that hold it still. What she retains instead are fragments: the sound of the walk-in refrigerator door, a particular angle of fluorescent light, the cold of the stainless steel counter pressing against her back, and a bodily knowledge so complete that when any of these fragments surface, she feels her body curl and brace as though the event is still happening. The memory does not come as story. It comes as posture.

In the months that followed, Ingrid found that the assault had not simply left a wound — it had rewritten the terms by which she understood other people. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like hard-won wisdom, that trust is a vulnerability that gets exploited. She had trusted this man. She had worked beside him for years, shared meals with him, advocated for his promotion. The betrayal was not incidental to her suffering; it was its centre. From this conviction — that people cannot be trusted, that harm can come from anyone, that she had been naive to believe otherwise — her perception of threat had expanded outward. Strangers approaching the pass-through window at the restaurant now activated a vigilance she could not override. Any unexpected movement nearby — a line cook turning suddenly, a server reaching past her — produced a full-body startle response that left her shaking and embarrassed. She was superalert at all times, scanning exits, tracking the position of every man in the room.

This state of chronic watchfulness fed directly back into her memory. When Ingrid was on high alert — which was most of her working day — the fragments came more readily, more insistently, and with them the physical reenactment: the bracing, the constriction in her chest, the sense of weight. The hypervigilance that was meant to protect her instead kept returning her to the very experience she was trying to outrun. And each time the memory surfaced in that embodied, wordless way, her conviction deepened — people cannot be trusted, she is not safe, the world confirmed this — which in turn sharpened her threat perception further, tightening the whole arrangement.

She began avoiding situations at work that she could not fully control. She stopped taking closing shifts. She refused to be in the walk-in refrigerator with any male colleague present, a change that her sous-chef noticed and that has generated friction on the team. Certain conversation topics — anything touching on workplace relationships, on loyalty, on what happened that night — caused her to go silent or leave the room. When her husband tried to draw her out emotionally, to get close in the way they once had, she found herself pulling back sharply; emotional intimacy had become a trigger in its own right, a reminder of the openness she had shown the man who harmed her. These appraisals of danger and betrayal were not only conclusions she had reached — they were lenses that actively shaped which situations felt unbearable, which conversations felt like threats, which moments of closeness felt like exposure.

What finally brought Ingrid to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when she snapped at a young male apprentice who had touched her shoulder to get her attention. She saw his face — startled, confused, a little hurt — and recognised something she did not want to become. She is most afraid that she is permanently changed. She hopes, tentatively, to find a way back to the kitchen she once loved.
